title: Decision trees, forests & boosting
summary: A practical family of models for structured data, nonlinear interactions, and strong baselines.
html:
A practical family of models for structured data, nonlinear interactions, and strong baselines.

How the pieces connect

Trees partition feature space

A decision tree chooses splits that make child nodes more homogeneous under an objective. Following splits routes a sample to a leaf with a prediction. Depth, minimum leaf size, and pruning limit complexity. Trees can model interactions without manually enumerating every feature combination.

Random forests reduce variance

A forest fits many trees using randomized samples and feature choices, then aggregates predictions. Diversity reduces correlated errors. More trees often stabilize predictions but increase memory and inference work. Out-of-bag estimates can be useful under their sampling assumptions; they do not replace an appropriate temporal or grouped holdout.

Boosting corrects residual mistakes

Gradient boosting adds weak learners sequentially to reduce an objective. Learning rate, tree count, leaf complexity, and subsampling control capacity. Early stopping uses a validation set. Modern implementations optimize histograms, missing-value handling, and hardware efficiency.

Interpretation requires care

Feature importance can favor high-cardinality variables or distribute credit unpredictably among correlated features. Permutation importance measures a change in predictive performance under a particular perturbation. Partial dependence can evaluate unrealistic combinations when features are correlated.

Worked example

MethodHow learners combineMain tradeoff
Single treeOne partitionReadable when small; unstable when deep
Random forestAverage randomized treesRobust baseline; larger model
Gradient boostingSequential corrective additionsStrong fit; careful tuning and leakage control

What goes wrong

Training deep trees until error vanishes invites overfitting. A feature that predicts well may be a leakage channel or a proxy, not a causal driver.

Check your understanding

Why does averaging identical trees give little benefit?

Reveal the explanation

Their errors are perfectly correlated. Ensembles gain from useful diversity, not just repeated copies.

An operating model for decision trees, forests & boosting

Trees are powerful because they create interactions and nonlinear regions without feature engineering, but every split is a chance to memorize an accident of the sample. Forests reduce variance through diverse trees; boosting reduces residual error through sequential trees. The choice depends on data size, noise, latency, and explainability needs.

The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test.

Worked system: a feature importance can be a proxy story

A tree ensemble assigns high importance to “number of account logins.” It is tempting to infer that frequent logins cause retention. But the feature may be a proxy for a paid plan, a region, a customer-support intervention, or a post-outcome event that leaked into the data. Trees are excellent at exploiting predictive structure and do not distinguish a useful signal from a causal explanation.

Probe importance by perturbing a feature, retraining on different splits, and comparing with a simpler model. Examine correlated features as a group: a tree may choose one arbitrary member of a correlated set and make it look uniquely decisive. Use the model to prioritize investigation, then return to the underlying process before making a policy claim.

Notebook: Measure the decision boundary, not only accuracy

Plot validation performance against depth or boosting rounds and use early stopping. Recompute feature attribution under perturbed data or alternate splits before treating it as an explanation.

from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix
tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred).ravel()
precision = tp / (tp + fp)
recall = tp / (tp + fn)
print({"precision": precision, "recall": recall})
What to test next. 1. Partition: A tree selects feature conditions. 2. Regularize: Depth, leaves, and sampling control capacity. 3. Combine: Average or sequentially correct weak learners. 4. Inspect: Test importances and errors against leakage and proxies.

The gotcha. A small inspection script proves only the quantities it prints. Preserve units, shapes, versions, and the input fixture beside its output.

A rigorous way to practice

  1. Partition. A tree selects feature conditions.
  2. Regularize. Depth, leaves, and sampling control capacity.
  3. Combine. Average or sequentially correct weak learners.
  4. Inspect. Test importances and errors against leakage and proxies.

Plot validation performance against depth or boosting rounds and use early stopping. Recompute feature attribution under perturbed data or alternate splits before treating it as an explanation.

Verification questions for decision trees, forests & boosting

BoundaryQuestionEvidence
PartitionWhat would show that this boundary failed?A tree selects feature conditions.
RegularizeWhat would show that this boundary failed?Depth, leaves, and sampling control capacity.
CombineWhat would show that this boundary failed?Average or sequentially correct weak learners.
InspectWhat would show that this boundary failed?Test importances and errors against leakage and proxies.

The gotcha. Passing each component check separately does not prove the composed path preserves identity, units, ordering, or authority.

Trees partition data; ensembles control their instability

A decision tree repeatedly chooses a feature condition that improves an impurity or loss objective. Deep trees adapt closely to data and can change substantially after a small sample perturbation.

  • Random forests reduce variance. Bootstrap samples and feature subsampling decorrelate trees, then averaging stabilizes prediction.
  • Boosting follows residual structure. Sequential learners correct current error and require learning-rate, depth, and stopping controls.
  • Missing values and categories are algorithm-specific. Native routing, encoding, and imputation produce different splits and leakage risks.
  • Importance is not causality. Gain, split count, permutation, and SHAP answer different model questions and react differently to correlated features.

The gotcha. A proxy feature can dominate prediction precisely because the ensemble is good at exploiting it.
